Who has attained success by correctly assigning, for each specific latent tendency, its particular object, its specific mode of activity, and its distinct classification, as you have analyzed them? Or who,
by applying [the analysis] in such and such a manner, has not achieved accomplishment therein?

If even the desire to know does not exist here, [then what else could?]. Through the discernment of the two paths— the path of the pure and the impure, and the path of compassion and the other— there arises the knowledge that distinguishes between the two ways.

Even among views, [that which is] established as the limit... where there is no mental distress, where tranquility is the chariot, and vision is free from darkness, moving toward the city [of liberation]—[this is the highest]. 12.
[the] non-clinging, free from substrate, ... the best means, Nirvana, the knowledge of the directions, ... the teacher himself. // 13
The vehicle has been revealed; the directions have been shown to be fearless;
the path for travelers has been granted; and that which was to be seen by those seeking liberation has been displayed.
If you have set out for liberation, what else remains for you? Who still harbors doubt, or in what matter, whose uncertainty has not been dispelled by you?
Who, having taken refuge in your teaching, has not been liberated from the bonds of existence?
Who could be restrained on the path?
What being was seen by you that has not been seen many times before?
Who, having accepted your dharma, has attained the state of a petitioner?
Who was the vessel for whose virtues he did not bestow [favor], in whom he did not act?
Whose intense longing did he not fulfill? And when [the goal] was attained, who was it that you did not lead to the end of the world? 16
Some were spoken of by him having approached them himself; some were entrusted [to others];
some were made [his] dependents right there;
and some were made his co-residents (*sahāyīkṛta*). Income was [secured], and [expenses] were reduced.
When [the requisites] have fallen away,
[he provides] them again; having prepared excellent food with supreme wealth for those who have arrived, he is capable of bringing happiness to those worthy of it.
O you whose banner is the Dharma, may they be established in your mind. ... having approached, even those who have drawn near... [18] ... x x x x m upetya ye 'py upa x x x x x x x x x.

...acting without guile, ... through qualities free from attachment, ... rain fell upon his eyes, and the true Dharma [pervaded] the sky.

...the True Dharma... // 20 ...by one who established himself [in it], why was the company of women avoided? Why were young men placed on the auspicious path, and why were children and the elderly excluded from without?
By drawing away those who are healthy, have you not abandoned those who are deranged, intoxicated, or afflicted?
Is there some interval where your subtle policy has not entered?
And why is it that even among those [who are] like illusions, the illusionist does not deceive them?
Why was the method of the lute not taught as being free from the defect of extremes regarding energy?
Why were the times when the mind is not supported by tranquility and equanimity not shown?
And having attained [enlightenment], why did you not act for the world’s welfare, which would have been appropriate for you? (22)
Searching for faults... [and] searching for virtues—what is the use of this? Are you constantly striving for evil against those who are striving for your welfare?
While they are asleep, why do you not keep watch?... [and] why do you not...?
Why are you weary of this people’s failure to discipline themselves, their grasping at the hair of those who have no protector?
Why do you despise these people in service? They do not desire to kill; they have not been made your own sons, yet when they have rebelled, [you treat them as such].
Indeed, your entire vision is permeated with compassion for the world;
those who were consumed by the darkness of evil thoughts and stood apart from you have now, O Protector, taken refuge in you, while those who were exalted by Māra have been brought low. (25)
Whatever merchandise of true merit has been acquired by me through praising You, O Conqueror of Death, may it deliver this final birth of mine from rebirth;
and may those people who dwell in saṃsāra, held fast by various fetters, [be delivered as well].
May there never be for them any births except those characterized by reliance upon the Three Jewels.
Thus ends the *Anaparāddhastotra*, the work of the venerable master Mātṛceṭa.

While some might even find fault in you,
you instead show yourself greater compassion toward him, just as a mother does for her own sick child.
This world is indifferent to the suffering of others and is solely distressed by its own suffering;
you, however, disregarding your own sufferings, are always distressed by the suffering of others.
O virtuous one, even through the sacrifice of their own lives, those sufferings which you endured did not produce for them the same joy that you felt.
...this world is not so afflicted as you are, whose mental continuum is tender with compassion, by the sufferings of others.
...a further act of grace toward the two princes,
like the favor bestowed by one whose mind is filled with compassion upon his left and right eyes.
O Sage, one would carry even the dust from your feet upon the crown of one's head;
for every action of yours overflows with the touchstone of compassion.
O steadfast one, though repeatedly tormented and even cut to pieces,
you did not undergo any transformation, like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.

...in the whirlpool of calamities, she who is compassionate and affectionate toward beings did not abandon you for even a moment, just as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) never abandons the phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, the faults such as intolerance and the like, though constantly attached to you,
were unable to overwhelm you...

I bow my head to that Sun of the Jina, who has created [this teaching] that destroys the darkness of ignorance.
Because of its profundity,
even the foremost [beings] stumbled;
because it was well-expounded, they attained youth.
...mita [the measured], possessing a most marvelous intellect.
Who would not bow their head to that best of debaters, whose well-expounded meaning is more profound than the ocean?
Today, his doctrine has been understood by those of but two-fingered intelligence.
[He is] quickly [overcome] by the possession of afflictions through [the influence of] women.
He who, by means of the weapons of patience, knowledge, and absolute cessation, conquered here the Māras known as Death, the Aggregates, Afflictions, and the God of Wine—
he likewise subdued the others directly.
Who would not worship him who has attained his own purpose and the purpose of others?
He who, with the waters of the auspicious Dharma, brought peace to those beings whose livers were scorched by the fierce flames of the great fire of the afflictions.
I pay homage to that sage-megha, who is like a mass of water.

I bow my head to him who made Nanda a servant— he who, at the moment when [the world] was immersed in the initiation of gazing upon his beloved’s face, received the command of Māra and brought it to pass.
I bow to that one who is joined with those who have fallen [into the world].
By the power of entering from one state to another, he who was Aṅgulimāla, situated in the midst of the garlands of flames of the fire of wrath, [fell] with a clashing descent...
[x x x x x x x].
I bow to him, the leader who carries others across the wilderness.
To him who, having gone to Urubilvā at the edge of the peaceful forest, performed the removal of the hair and afflictions of the matted-hair ascetics—
to that perfected one, the supreme king of the Vidyādharas.
Homage be to the one who destroys the poison of various views and afflictions!
By means of supernatural powers, by some through infallible instructions and mental admonitions, and by others through various other skillful means, he—
who possesses manifold forms— trained those who were to be tamed among men.
I pay homage to that one, the great charioteer of the world.
To those who had fallen into the river of craving, whose banks were eroded by the waters of the afflictions and which was filled with many terrors from the crocodiles of dogmatic views,
he extended the long hand of compassion, which was wisdom.
To him, the protector and the savior, I bow down.

For those beings who, under the sway of the onset of false knowledge, are powerless, whose courses are cast into the whirlpools of birth, and who have no refuge— he [is the one] who [knows] the means of escape from the miserable states (apāya).
To those who were leaning forward, he, desiring their welfare, said: "He is my refuge."
He who, having gone to them, performed such unrequited services for the world as if by force,
treating them as friends, a protector, a kinsman, a noble one, a teacher, and a lord— [to him, x + 11].
Indeed, never satiated, I bow down to him again and again.
From the midst of the ocean of the Buddha’s qualities, we have extracted this single drop through devotion and exertion;
may the merit obtained from this today be shared equally with all beings.
May all sentient beings partake in the nectar of the true reality of phenomena.

Śārdūlavikrīḍita)
Mandākrāntā; Lévi 1929) 3:
Having attained perfection for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I now bear this very body solely for the welfare of sentient beings.
For how can he who harms sentient beings even in his mind rely upon me alone, being indifferent toward me?
But that indeed is worship which, even when directed toward the welfare of sentient beings, brings satisfaction to the mind of the one worthy of worship;
whereas that which is violent in nature, or arises from the intent to harm others, is not.
Even when performed with refinement, worship does not follow that which is to be worshipped.
Wives, sons, wealth, high status, and sovereignty;
flesh, blood, eyes, and the body—
all these were abandoned by me on account of that which is dear.
Whoever harms them, by that I am harmed.
6. For my supreme worship consists in benefiting sentient beings, and my utter defeat would consist in harming sentient beings.

Having encountered sentient beings, I have performed virtuous deeds and propitiated the Protectors;
I have attained the perfections while remaining dedicated solely to the welfare of the assembly of sentient beings.
With a mind exerted for the sake of sentient beings, the power of Māra was shattered.
It was by sentient beings alone, through their various acts of creation, that I was made into a Buddha.
Upon what object can compassion and loving-kindness be established here?

Upon what should they be focused, and upon what objects such as equanimity and sympathetic joy? For whose sake were patience cultivated for so long with a mind intent on compassion? And where are the liberations and the rest?
If living beings were not friends in the performance of pleasant deeds in birth after birth, they would not exist as such.
It was sentient beings alone who, having taken on the states of elephants and other forms, were given by me on countless occasions;
and it was sentient beings alone who, having become worthy recipients, were made to accept my gifts.
Through sentient beings alone, by virtue of their passage through various states of existence, my compassion has been increased.
If I do not protect sentient beings themselves, for whose sake has any purpose been accomplished?
If sentient beings had not become habituated to the world of Yama through the mockery of the whirlpools of birth in this saṃsāra, which abounds in the onset of calamities,
then this crossing over from saṃsāra— this Buddhistic majesty— would be nothing short of most wonderful.
For whose sake would there be any striving, if sentient beings were not dear to me?
"As long as this teaching of mine, which illuminates the world, continues to burn, so long must you— who possess yourselves and are devoted to the welfare of others— remain [in this world].
Having heard this again and again..."
My resolve is for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, you who are untiring should not cause weariness to this body of mine, which has already been described as being of little substance.
The Mahāyāna sūtra entitled "Pleasing Beings," spoken by the Samyaksambuddha, is completed.
“Epithets of the Buddha” (Schlingloff 1955: 82f.):

... [he who is] possessed of the three types of knowledge (*trividyā*), the knower of the three times (*trikālajña*), [the one who has] the three... / [he who is] perfected in the three miracles (*triprātihāryasaṃpanna*), and the teacher of the words of the three aggregates (*triskandhapadadeśika*) // (8)
... free from fever, a leader, without "mine-ness," and without egoism; ... and blameless, as well as free from worldly existence; ... the supreme among men. (10b)
Endowed with knowledge and conduct, the one who has transcended all passions, whose mind is disciplined, the best among those who know the words [of the Dharma];
he who has stilled [all things], whose evil is pacified, who has become cool, and who brings about auspiciousness.
The Teacher, the refuge of the world, the source of [all things],
endowed with the auspicious marks of a śramaṇa, glorious, and devoted to the welfare of the world.
Compassionate toward all beings, having crossed over [the ocean of existence], his every desire fulfilled, he is auspicious and happy. 17
*Munayastava* (Schlingloff 1955: 85–88, including the additions by Pauly in *JA* 1957:
304 and 1959: 227, and the unpublished fragment).
Homage to that great seer, the sage, the protector of the world, the hero among men, the wise one who knows the inclinations of all sentient beings. (Pelliot Skt. bleu 164, verse 1)
Homage to that seeker of the welfare of others, by whom this world, seeing it ablaze with the fire of the afflictions, was quenched with the water of wisdom;
he whose conduct— whether of speech, body, or mind— is entirely free from error.
Homage be to him who is liberated from all faults, whose karma is undefiled!
Homage to that Lord of Men, who has crossed the vast ocean of the knowable with the arms of wisdom, and whose prowess and intellect are incomparable!
Salutations to him who possesses stainless vision, the knower of all phenomena, by whom this entire object of knowledge was seen with the eye of his own intellect.
He is the most excellent among all beings, arising from the excellence of their fortune, form, and qualities.
Homage be to him who possesses the five powers of the two-fold nature, the one who is without rival.
Homage to that stainless Arhat who has mastery over his own mind, whose thought functions with equal impartiality toward both an enemy and a child.
Homage to that Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū), who, having himself emerged after piercing the egg of delusion with the beak of wisdom,
is free from all attachments; homage to him who has withdrawn the senses and moves within the range of primordial knowledge.

Homage to that virtuous one who possesses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Homage to that illustrious one who has been praised and honored by Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, Āditya, Yakṣas, Asuras, humans, and serpents.
Homage to him who, with the eye of wisdom, has seen the four truths; to him whose mind is purified, and to that [teaching] which [he proclaimed].
Homage to him by whom sensual pleasure was seen as being like poison, fire, and a serpent.

// 12 Homage to him whose nature is peace, who knows the dispositions and latent tendencies, who reveals the path and the non-path, and who is free from possessiveness and attachment! // 13

Homage to him whose mind is never defiled by faults such as passion; to him who is pure, self-controlled, and whose dust has been stilled. Homage to that great Peaceful One, who perceives the true meaning of the teachings.
Homage be to the one who has attained liberation, who is free from evil, and whose mind is incomparable!
Homage to that wise one who proclaims the peerless Dharma, which is well-composed, appropriate, and beautiful in its beginning, middle, and end! (15–16)
Homage to him who possesses the three eyes, who is liberated from the three afflictions, who dwells in the three concentrations, and who is freed from the three worlds;
homage to the auspicious one, whose virtue is pure, the illustrious son of the Śākyas.
Homage to him who has attained peace, the refuge for those seeking tranquility.
Homage to that King of Dharma, who possesses mastery over all aims, whose command remains unconfused even here in this world despite his having entered nirvāṇa.

Homage to that radiant one, whose form shines with the brilliance of gold, by whose splendor the moon, fire, and sun are rendered lusterless; homage to him who is endowed with all purposeful qualities and who has compassion for all living beings.
Homage to the one who has accomplished all aims, who desires the welfare of all sentient beings.
Homage to that Great Soul, whose limit of qualities cannot be known through inference, nor by comparison, nor by the untainted [states], nor by mere reasoning.
By whatever merit has been gained by praising me with hundreds of hymns using the fourth case-ending,
may that merit lead all sentient beings to the realization of the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
The *Munayastava* is completed.
Rāhulastava (Schlingloff 1955: 89–92):
O Essence of Beings, homage to you, whose pure and incomparable awakening is such that, in all circumstances, you are devoted solely to the welfare of the world. (1)
That resolve which first arose in you out of compassion, desiring to deliver the world— truly, that was a most great marvel.
Just as that initial thought for enlightenment arose in you, so too [should it remain].
In that very same way, you are worthy of worship by this world and stand above it.
(3) It is said that the virtuous strive to protect those who have come to them for refuge; yet you have risen to protect this entire world, even though it has not sought refuge in you. (4)
"Your wondrous resolve, renowned throughout the three worlds,

is such that people of little merit, being weak of soul, are not even capable of hearing of it. For in this world, there are those who care only for themselves and are indifferent to the welfare of others."
"How will your mind find satisfaction in such noble resolve?
For this entire world of living beings, with its diverse intentions and activities, desires and imitates actions that correspond to its own nature. (6–7)
O Sage, that resolve of yours, born of compassion, which arose previously to protect this afflicted world, was in accordance with your own being;
for though you knew the sufferings of saṃsāra and were capable of going to nirvāṇa, [you did not do so].
For a long time you have been afflicted in saṃsāra, solely out of compassion.
Whether born in the world of the gods, the world of men, or anywhere else,
compassion has never left you, just as a mother does not abandon her own biological son.
Though tormented by the unbearable sufferings easily found in saṃsāra,
you did not release your resolve, clinging to it as if to your own kinsman.
Whatever merit you performed through the actions of mind, speech, and body, [you did so with that same intent].
O compassionate one, you have performed this solely for the sake of others.
Your own task is the task of others, and the suffering of others is what troubles you;
